headline: High: Cline’s workspace/file and browser tooling can feed Pipecat’s shared-bus, API-backed pipelines, creating default-path prompt, leakage, and cascading-error risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cline reads and writes workspace files and can use MCP, while Pipecat runs with a shared bus/session model and ingests text/audio/video streams. A direct injection bridge is plausible if Cline outputs are forwarded into Pipecat inputs or shared files, but the pairwise path is inferred rather than directly documented.
conditions: IF Cline-generated text is routed into Pipecat prompts or transcripts without sanitization
IF both agents share a filesystem or message bus that carries instructions as data
mitigations: Add an explicit instruction/data delimiter in the handoff format
Strip tool directives from Cline outputs before forwarding
Disable shared-bus forwarding for untrusted content
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to every message

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cline touches source code and browser screenshots in a per-workspace session, while Pipecat handles text, audio, video, images, and conversation state over a shared bus. If the same workspace or bus carries sensitive artifacts, either agent can expose them through its outbound API calls; the exact leakage path is inferred from profiles, not observed.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or screenshots are placed on the shared bus or in a shared workspace
IF Pipecat forwards conversation state to third-party STT/LLM/TTS services
mitigations: Keep Cline and Pipecat on separate workspaces
Remove secrets and screenshots before handoff
Restrict Pipecat connectors to local-only services
Rotate any exposed API keys
requires-engineering: enforce per-message data-class labels

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cline has broad filesystem write, shell, and git mutation in a workspace-scoped session; Pipecat supports shared-bus concurrency across processes and machines. If both touch the same mutable project state, concurrent writes and git changes can collide by default, and the profiles do not show locking or coordination.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git repository
IF Pipecat instances and Cline run without external locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Pause one agent during commits or file rewrites
Use a single writer for git state
Add a lockfile around shared mutations
requires-engineering: introduce transactional workspace coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cline can generate code, browser-derived facts, and file edits; Pipecat can consume text and drive downstream voice or API services. If Pipecat treats Cline output as authoritative, an upstream mistake can cascade into spoken, logged, or API-mediated actions. No verification step is documented in either profile.
conditions: IF Pipecat consumes Cline output without validation
IF downstream Pipecat services act on that output in production
mitigations: Insert a human review step before actioning outputs
Require schema validation on all handoffs
Limit Pipecat to read-only summarization of Cline output
Log and diff every transformed message
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking gates

E_compliance.rationale: Cline handles model-provider API keys and browser screenshots, while Pipecat processes audio, video, images, text, and conversation state with multiple third-party service integrations. The profiles do not specify residency, retention, or certification alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven; uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PII, PHI, or customer recordings flows through Pipecat connectors
IF retention or residency requirements differ between the two deployment environments
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared flows
Document retention for each connector
Disable analytics exports where possible
Confirm residency for every third-party API
requires-engineering: align DPA and retention controls
